realLife: Colour reduction in images, customer segments and grouping sensor readings all use k-means because it is fast and easy to explain.
summary: Drop k centres, pull each point to its nearest one, move the centres, repeat.
headline: Centres that chase their own points
overview: k-means starts with k centres. Every point joins its nearest centre, then each centre moves to the average of its points. Those two steps repeat until nothing changes.

The number k is your guess. Inertia, the total squared distance to the centres, always shrinks as k grows, so it cannot tell you the right k by itself. Silhouette, which compares how close a point is to its own group versus the next nearest, gives a second opinion.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Run k-means on two concentric rings. It can only cut with straight lines between centres, so each ring is split in half instead of separated from the other.

check.question: Why can't you choose k by picking the lowest inertia?
options: Inertia always falls as k rises, reaching zero when every point is its own cluster
Inertia cannot be computed for large k

data: One hundred and fifty unlabelled points in 2D from four shapes. The true groups are kept aside only to score agreement. Starting centres come from k-means++ unless you switch to random.
maths: a is the mean distance to the point's own cluster, b the mean distance to the nearest other cluster. k-means always converges, but possibly to a local minimum, which is why scikit-learn offers k-means++ starts and repeated runs.
code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
m = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
m.inertia_, silhouette_score(X, m.labels_)
